sermon.title: Saul: The Haunted House
sermon.thesis: Saul is Judah before Judah: religion used as a tool, an empty house that gets occupied.

outline.text: 1. The kind of person who uses religion

outline.body: Some people use religion for the advantages it brings. Saul is that kind of person.
Matthew 12:43–45 — the house empty, swept, and put in order, then occupied by seven worse spirits. “So also will it be with this evil generation.”
Self-interest is a real part of our relationship with God. Deuteronomy is full of promises of blessing, so wanting blessing doesn’t prove you’re Saul.
David loved blessing too (Psalm 16:5–6, 11; Psalm 27:4, 13). So what’s the difference, and how do I know?
Chapter 9: lost donkeys. Saul doesn’t know Samuel (9:18). To Saul, the seer is a service.

The forks. Each time obedience looks like the bad idea, he picks the blessing over the Blesser: Gilgal (13:8–12, “I forced myself”); the ark and the rash oath (14:18–19, 24, 44); Amalek (15:21–24, 30, “I feared the people”).
We never hear Saul talk about God the way David does — it is “the LORD your God” (15:15, 21, 30).
David at the same forks: he spares Saul in the cave and the camp (1 Samuel 24, 26), sends the ark back while fleeing Absalom (2 Samuel 15:25–26), and lets Shimei curse (2 Samuel 16).
Then the house is occupied: the Spirit departs and a harmful spirit comes (16:14). Jealousy, the spear, Nob (chapter 22).
Saul’s experiences were real — the Spirit rushed on him, he was given another heart, he prophesied, he won at Jabesh. Experience alone doesn’t settle it.
Hebrews 6:4–8 — enlightened, tasted, shared in the Spirit, then fell away. Same rain, different ground; rain isn’t fruit.
Hebrews 6:9 — “In your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things.” Assurance for the tender, warning for the comfortable. Gifted is not the same as indwelt (cf. Matthew 7:22).
Saul’s life opens and closes at a seer’s door, trying to use the spiritual for a personal need: the donkeys (chapter 9) and the medium at Endor (chapter 28).
1 Chronicles 10:13–14 — he died for breaking faith and consulting a medium, “and did not seek guidance from the LORD.” Compare Ichabod (1 Samuel 4:21–22): the ark carried as a charm.

outline.text: Application 1: Who you are when you suffer

outline.body: Who you are when you suffer is who you are (1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:3; Genesis 22:1). You may need a moment to get your legs under you — that’s normal. But who you are over the long haul of hurting is who you are.

outline.text: Application 2: Saul as an institutional problem

outline.body: Saul personifies what will dominate Judah by Isaiah’s day: obedience vs. sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11–15); inquiring of the dead (Isaiah 8:19); Ahaz at the fork (Isaiah 7:9); “like the nations” — Egypt and horses (Isaiah 30–31); lips near, heart far (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8).
Hezekiah takes the David road (Isaiah 37). The King who finally passes every fork comes in Isaiah 11 and 53.
Saul asked the dead. Ask the living God. Seek him for what you must do to be saved, not for the donkeys. Ask him to show you whether religion has been a tool for you.
Christ took the fork perfectly — the wilderness (Matthew 4), Gethsemane, obedience learned through suffering (Hebrews 5:7–8). The house he fills is not haunted (Ephesians 2:22).

announcements.title: Men's Retreat
announcements.body: Men, mark your calendars for our annual Men's Retreat. Meet Justin Lackmacher, founder of Redemption House. Chris and Dov have gotten to know Justin over the years and are absolutely thrilled to have him spend time with the men at Providence. Justin is a former addict, a current minister to addicts, and — as Pastor Chris puts it — has serious Biblical Counseling game. Spots are limited; registration cost increases on October 12.
